[[RunningHead]]

Report on the 20th Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society, Brussels, Belgium, 2019: “Satisfaction at last: Neuropsychoanalysis on sex, drive, and enjoyment”

Daniela Flores Mosri

Daniela Flores Mosri

Mexico City
Mexico
Psychology, Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy and Neuropsychoanalysis

Daniela Flores Mosri   CONTACT Daniela Flores Mosri dannmos@yahoo.com

Introduction

The 20th Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society took place in Brussels, Belgium, from July 18th to 20th 2019. The Congress was held at the Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB) and covered the topic “Satisfaction at last. Neuropsychoanalysis on sex, drive, and enjoyment.” People from many countries attended, including Lebanon, Japan, Austria, the United States, Portugal, Ireland, Sweden, Germany, the United Kingdom, Israel, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Turkey, Slovenia, Lithuania, Canada, Mexico, Spain, the Czech Republic, Peru, Romania, South Africa, Switzerland, Brazil, Norway, Taiwan, Japan, Hong Kong, India, Finland, Republic of Korea, Poland, Puerto Rico, Greece, Latvia, Australia, New Zealand, and Uruguay. This report summarizes the main contents of the keynote talks. For further details, the reader is referred to the speakers' publications.

Day one

The Congress was preceded by an Educational Day to introduce the topic of sex, drive, and enjoyment with four talks. Oliver Turnbull was first and spoke about the neuroscience of sexuality. His talk was divided into two main sections. The first described the subjective experience of sex, and the second focused on the variations of sexual orientation and gender identity. The first part began with a description of the phases of the sexual cycle, following the work of Masters and Johnson (1966), which are (1) excitement or arousal, (2) plateau, (3) orgasm, and (4) resolution or refractory period. Turnbull suggested that the first two stages, i.e. arousal and plateau, could be put together. He emphasized that the study of the subjective experience of sex is neglected in the literature. He claimed that neuropsychoanalysis is ideal to discuss this aspect. Turnbull described the phase of arousal as desire and excitement triggered by thoughts and erogenous touch. Psychologically speaking, there is an increase of energy and enthusiasm, and other types of stimuli are neglected to focus on the object of desire. The second phase, plateau, is characterized by an even more emphatic increase in energy and desire. The phase of orgasm is featured by feelings of pleasure and relief all over the body, but particularly at the genitals. The feeling lasts for a few seconds and then declines. For the mind it is a period of loss of energy and relaxation, accompanied by feelings of attachment and fondness for the other person. Turnbull then discussed the plateau or arousal phase versus the resolution phase. He termed the chemistries released before orgasm the before chemistries, and those that follow orgasm the after chemistries. He described that wanting and liking, as characterized by Berridge, are both pleasurable, but in different ways. He related erogenous zones to affective or affiliative touch, which is mediated by C-tactile fibers or afferents that go to the cortex. Turnbull spoke of the distribution of erogenous zones in the primary somatosensory cortex. He reminded the audience of Ramachandran’s theory about the location of some parts of the body in the somatosensory cortex, such as the genitals and the feet next to each other. Ramachandran then concluded that the feet are erogenous owing to that. Turnbull investigated the topic and disproved Ramachandran’s idea, given that the somatosensory cortex is not erogenous. Stimulating that area produces sensations of tickling or scratching, but not erotic sensations. Turnbull added that the feet are not fetish object choices; he clarified that fetishists are indifferent to the touch of their own feet because fetish object choices are related to visual aspects. Fetish object choices vary amongst individuals as opposed to erogenous zones which are shared by all 139

Charlotte Kahn

Charlotte Kahn   c.kahn@rcn.com

It is always a lovely surprise to see new movements inside the variety of the regional groups. The themes and variations of each group demonstrates quite well how we are turning the application of consilience into a well-established practice in our Society. In this report, I particularly highlight the report of the work done by the Turkish Neuropsychoanalysis Study Group (Cross-cultural Affective Neuroscience Personality Comparisons of Japan, Turkey and Germany. Culture and Brain, Fatma Gökçe Özkarar-Gradwohl). Read on for a taste of the results of their transcultural study, supervised by Prof. Jaak Panksepp.

I look forward to our congress in Brussels this July, where we can celebrate two decades together!

Bulletin 37

The Neuropsychoanalysis Group of Mexico City

2018 was a stimulating and busy year in Mexico in terms of neuropsychoanalysis. Mexico City hosted the 19th Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society at the Universidad Intercontinental from August 31st to September 2nd, giving a large local and international audience the chance to enjoy interesting presentations on the topic of Repression and Defense. During November, Mark Solms returned to Mexico City to facilitate a clinical workshop.

The group continued its study group sessions exploring topics such as consciousness, and emotional memory. Israel Grande gave a compelling lecture on minimal self-consciousness. Neuropsychiatrist Leonardo Ruiz gave a brilliant talk about the neurobiology of laughter and humor. Dr. Hans Olvera gave an original presentation about intrauterine stimulation and its relation to psychic inscription. The last session covered the mental apparatus and a discussion regarding Mark Solms’ model of the conscious id.

Dr. Xavier Sánchez Guzmán presented his research about Parkinson’s disease and its relation to narcissistic depressions at the Universidad Intercontinental. Dr. Daniela Flores Mosri gave a keynote lecture regarding the validity of psychoanalysis to date from a neuropsychoanalytic perspective in Mexicali at the CETYS. She also gave a workshop and participated in a discussion session. Later in the year, she gave several lectures on addiction, adolescence, and anxiety.

[[RunningHead]]

20 years of neuropsychoanalysis: Reflections from regional groups

Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner   magsterz@gmail.com

The regional groups of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society have been a vital part of the body of neuropsychoanalysis, as Fatma Gke zkarar Gradwohl says in her reflection below. These groups of clinicians and researchers have been gathering together to study neuroscience and psychoanalysis for several decades now, incubating new perspectives on clinical work, generating new empirical research, hosting conferences, and producing a wide range of publications. Many of these groups have included some of the most dedicated and involved members of our community. We invited the group coordinators to contribute their reflections on how neuropsychoanalysis has affected them and their members over the years, and the responses give a flavour of the ways in which our interdisciplinary endeavour have enriched their lives, and how the groups have in turn enriched international neuropsychoanalysis.

The Editors

[[RunningHead]]

Taphophobia and resurrection mania following left parietal stroke

Iftah Biran

Iftah Biran

Tel Aviv
Israel

Kadima
Israel

Iftah Biran   CONTACT Iftah Biran i_biran@hotmail.com Division of Neurology, Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center, 6 Weizmann St. Tel Aviv, 6423906, Israel
Angular gyrus, Cotard’s syndrome, heterotopagnosia, autotopagnosia, resurrection mania, taphophobia

The paper describes a patient with psychotic depression following left inferior parietal stroke. He had a dominant delusion: a belief that he was buried alive and had died thereafter. This delusion was an amalgamation of taphophobia (fear of being buried alive) and Cotard’s nihilistic delusion. This taphophobia-Cotard complex was accompanied by a resurrection delusional belief that his son would resuscitate him by pressing his chest through the gravestone, during which the son’s hands would be detached from his body. This uncanny presentation is analyzed on various levels: Psychiatric level with an attempt to understand this presentation as reactivation of post-traumatic stress disorder; classical neurological level based on the function of the left parietal cortex and its role in body representations as in Gerstmann’s syndrome; Coltheart’s neuropsychological “Two-Factors Model” of delusional beliefs suggesting that the nihilistic-like delusion stems from false interpretation secondary to impaired mental activity that follows similar brain lesions and that this interpretation is not rejected due to lack of censorship activity; psychodynamic level – looking at the switch to primary thinking processes and at the accompanying uncanniness, anxiety and manic defenses. The paper suggests that what seems like diverse and haphazard presentation can be a multifaceted expression of the crucial function of the left inferior parietal cortex as a heteromodal cortex sited in an intersection between concrete perceptions and symbolic constructs and between primary and secondary thinking processes.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Metapsychological consequences of the conscious brainstem: A critique of the conscious id

Volker Hartmann Cardelle

Volker Hartmann Cardelle

Independent Researcher

Volker Hartmann Cardelle   CONTACT Volker A. Hartmann Cardelle volker.hartmann@protonmail.com Gladbachstrasse 110, 8044 Zurich, Switzerland
Metapsychology, mental apparatus, consciousness, mind-brain problem, Mealy machine

In this article, the thesis that the id is conscious [Solms, (2013a) The conscious id. Neuropsychoanalysis, 15(1), 5–19] is scrutinized by carving out a crucial implicit assumption on which the argument relies. The validity of this assumption is then assessed in two ways: first by an analysis of Freud’s description of the relation between the mental apparatus and the brain, second by analyzing the neuropsychoanalytical implications of the Mealy machine [Mealy, 1955. A method for synthesizing sequential circuits. Bell Labs Technical Journal, 34(5), 1045–1079] – a mathematical model that is used to describe the relation between the software and hardware of computers. The result of my assessment is that Solms’s implicit assumption faces serious objections and therefore the conclusion that the id is conscious cannot be upheld. In the remaining article I develop, based on the neuroscientific findings on which Solms developed his thesis [Solms & Panksepp, 2012. The “id” knows more than the “ego” admits: Neuropsychoanalytic and primal consciousness perspectives on the interface between affective and cognitive neuroscience. Brain Sciences, 2(2), 147–175], a concurrent adaptation of the structural model. This is achieved by an analysis of Freud's development of his metapsychological theory from 1899 to 1923, with a strong focus on the conceptualization of consciousness that underwent, as I shall work out, a major change. The result is a new metapsychological model that, so I claim, gets rid of a crucial weak spot of the structural model [Freud, 1923. The ego and the id. Standard Edition, 19, 12–59] and allows the integration of different neuropsychological theories.

The 20th International Neuropsychoanalysis Congress, Brussels, 18-20 July, 2019: “Satisfaction at Last: Neuropsychoanalysis on Sex, Drive and Enjoyment”

Thursday, 18 July

Plenary symposium

Wherever Narcissus is, Echo had already been: Interdisciplinary perspectives on narcissism and sexuality (Chair: Aikaterini Fotopoulou)

Manos Tsakiris

The erogenous mirror: Interpersonal, multisensory, and mutual maps of sexual arousal

We take a novel interpersonal and multimodal approach to characterize the self-reported intensity and distribution of erogenous zones, mapped both on one’s own body and on an imagined partner’s body in response to being touched but also being looked at. Here we show the presence of a multimodal erogenous mirror between sexual partners, as we observed clear correspondences between individuals' topographic distributions of erogenous zones on their own and their partners' bodies, as well as between those elicited by touch and vision. The erogenous body is therefore organized and represented in an interpersonal and multisensory way. The implications of this organization are discussed in relation to current neuropsychoanalytic models of body-awareness.

Manos Tsakiris is Professor of Psychology at Royal Holloway, University of London. His research is highly interdisciplinary and uses a wide range of methods to investigate the neurocognitive mechanisms that shape the experience of embodiment and self-identity. He is the recipient of the Young Mind and Brain Prize in 2014, the 22nd Experimental Psychology Society Prize in 2015, and the NOMIS Foundation Distinguished Scientist Award in 2016.

Email: Manos.Tsakiris@rhul.ac.uk

[[RunningHead]]

Seeing without self: Discovering new meaning with psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy

Lawrence Fischman

Lawrence Fischman

Portland
ME
USA
Department of Psychiatry

Lawrence Fischman   CONTACT Lawrence G. Fischman lfisch55@gmail.com 153 Park Row, Brunswick, ME 04011, USA

Psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy, ego dissolution, default mode network, connectivity, mentalization

New research in psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy merits a reexamination of the neurobiology and phenomenology of psychedelic states. First person accounts of psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy are used to re-conceptualize the ego boundary as a defense mechanism which regulates the significance that objects hold for the self. Therapeutic action is attributed to ego dissolution, which enables subjects to see new significance in things. This process coincides neurobiologically with uncoupling certain midline cortical structures, and psychodynamically, with deactivating defense mechanisms which mitigate the threat of losing the loved object. It also enables the dreamlike imagery, symbols, and metaphor of the primary process, a regression to earlier ways of relating to objects, and feelings of love and connectivity. The process supports Freud's ideas about the oceanic mode of relating to the world existing alongside the narrower, mature ego feeling. The former is better suited for finding meaning in life, while the latter is better suited for survival. The noetic quality of the psychedelic state derives from an unconscious recognition that experiences without character defenses feel more genuine than others, and conform to earlier ways of feeling and thinking. The accessibility of the primary process makes psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy transformative, not just informative. An analogy is drawn to Fonagy's developmental model of mentalization. Absent the defensive, self-critical lens of a prior self-concept, psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy serves as an ideal paradigm for the transformative experience of seeing oneself through the eyes of another, leading to greater self-acceptance. Flight instructions for navigating this royal road to the unconscious are considered.

John Dall’Aglio

John Dall’Aglio

John Dall’Aglio   CONTACT John Dall’Aglio john_dallaglio@brown.edu Brown University, Providence, RI, United States of America Developmental Psychosomatics Laboratory, New York State Psychiatric Institute/Columbia University Medical Center, New York, NY, USA

Lacan, metapsychology, affective consciousness, real, imaginary, symbolic, neuropsychoanalysis, psychoanalysis

Meta-psychological bridges between neuroscience and psychoanalysis have focused on Freud’s structural model [Kaplan-Solms & Solms, 2002. Clinical studies in neuro-psychoanalysis: Introduction to a depth neuropsychology (2nd ed.). London: Karnac Books; Solms, 2013. The conscious id. Neuropsychoanalysis, 15(1), 5–19]. While other psychoanalytic schools have been in dialog on specific concepts, alternative full-scale meta-psychologies have received less attention. This paper maps the brain through the Lacanian triad of the real, imaginary, and symbolic. Dynamic localization of these concepts avoids neuro-structural reduction. Right and left cortical hemispheres appear necessary (but not sufficient) for imaginary and symbolic functions respectively, with the frontal lobes underlying social and self-reflective functions. The real is supported by subcortical affective and motivational structures, particularly the automatization of non-representational systems prior to hippocampal development. This project highlights the structural disjuncture (impossibility) which is constitutive of human subjectivity and brain function.

Reflections on 20 years of Neuropsychoanalysis

Ross Balchin , Virginia Barry , Ariane Bazan , Mark Blechner , Andrea Clarici , Daniela Mosri , Aikaterini Fotopoulou , Maria Goergen , Richard Kessler , Iréne Matthis , José Zúñiga , Georg Northoff , David Olds , Lois Oppenheim , Doris Reismann-Lagrèze , Manos Tsakiris , Doug Watt , Giles Yeates and Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner   mzellner@npsa-association.org

As this journal was founded in 1999, and the 20th Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society took place in 2019, this year seems a fitting time to celebrate the 20th anniversary of neuropsychoanalysis. The celebration was kicked off by an in-depth interview of Oliver Turnbull by Christian Salas in our previous issue. In what follows, other members of the neuropsychoanalysis community share some personal, social, and theoretical reflections on the importance of neuropsychoanalysis since the founding of the journal and the Society. Through personal histories, remembrances of the “pre-history” and development of the neuropsychoanalysis community, and discussions of concepts and findings that have emerged at our congresses and in these pages, a nuanced landscape of our vital, interdisciplinary project emerges. – The Editors

New perspectives and new resources

My wonderful and enriching journey in neuropsychoanalysis began sixteen years ago at the University of Cape Town when Professor Mark Solms walked into our first postgraduate lecture as trainee clinicians and proclaimed that we were about to learn a unique, yet fundamentally important approach to clinical neuropsychology. The dictum that I heard back then was underpinned by the following two key tenets, which clinical experience has subsequently shown me are crucial if one is to correctly understand, diagnose, and ultimately assist brain-injured patients.

First, the relatively novel (in the neuropsychology world at least) hypothetico-deductive approach dictates that, rather than merely measuring a patient's functions quantitatively and at face value using standardized tests (in short, a purely psychometric approach), the clinician must instead aspire to answering a clinical question by generating and then systematically excluding hypotheses in order to test and explore patients’ neurocognitive functions. In doing so, s/he can reach an accurate and practically meaningful clinical impression based on testing and then systematically excluding differential diagnoses. This approach demands careful and decided qualitative observations and the interpretation of clinical signs and symptoms in relation to the underlying brain pathology. This necessarily requires an understanding of neuroanatomical correlates of normal mental functions and how these relate to the specific neurocognitive disorders seen in patients. The clinical task must ultimately be to ensure that converging lines of evidence from the assessment process all point to one unifying clinical presentation. Practising in multilingual, multicultural South Africa, where the population also varies greatly in terms of level of education, as well as religious and cultural beliefs and customs, has further emphasized to me just how valuable, albeit sometimes challenging, this approach is, as one is obliged to also consider these additional multiple dimensions when reaching one's diagnostic conclusions.

Developments in metapsychology: Contributions to neuropsychoanalytic engagement with Freud, and new links to Lacan

Richard Kessler and Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner

New York City
NY
USA

New York City
NY
USA

Maggie Zellner   mzellner@npsa-association.org

Readers of Neuropsychoanalysis may have noticed that Freudian metapsychology appears to be alive and well. In this issue, we are pleased to publish two very stimulating neuro-metapsychological papers: one that makes a significant contribution to the ongoing development of Freudian ideas, and one which charts a path to doing the same with Lacan.

In his 1981 paper “Does metapsychology still exist?,” Arnold Modell regards metapsychology as referring to psychological phenomena of the highest generalizability – universal to the human species and thereby close to biological bedrock. Seen by Modell as a modeling device or an experiment in thinking, metapsychology provides the space where the “subjective” meets the “objective,” where the empathic identifier meets the naturalistic observer. From the beginning, Freud’s metapsychology of the mental apparatus drew from both the subjective and the objective, and was a conception of the mind that was informed by ideas about the brain – for example, Freud’s ideas in Chapter 7 of The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) is derived not just from the transformation of the explicitly neurologically-based Project (Solms & Saling, 1996), but also from his clinical experience. It is the product of a creative collision of careful listening to exquisitely individualistic and sometimes idiosyncratic utterances of patients with the understanding of the biological imperatives of human nature. In its foundation, therefore, metapsychology epitomizes the marriage of idiographic and nomothetic perspectives, a kind of double vision. The concept of the wish, for example, emerges not just from consideration of the infinite individual varieties of human desire, but also their grounding in the forces of self and species preservation. Today, our understanding of the wish is enriched by our knowledge of its relationship to the SEEKING system (Schonbachler, Stojkovic, & Boothe, 2016) and the evolutionary biology of REM sleep (Fisher & Kessler, 2018). Freud’s metapsychology overcomes the narrowly conceived boundaries of scientific disciplines. It is a “double-edged sword that enables creative and metaphorical thought about the mind’s hidden realities” (Bruner, 1994, p. 83).

20 years of neuropsychoanalysis

Richard Kessler , David Olds and Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner

New York City

New York City

New York City

Maggie Zellner   mzellner@npsa-association.org

This is quite a celebratory issue. Because this journal was founded in 1999, and the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society held its 20th Congress this year, we thought this year is a suitable time to celebrate two decades of neuropsychoanalysis.

These twenty years have been full of exciting meetings around the world, and an explosion of publications connecting the brain with psychoanalytic concepts – many of which have appeared in these pages. It has been a time of new ideas and of re-evaluating long-standing ones, sometimes supporting those older ideas in surprising ways, and sometimes updating or discarding them. Moreover, on a social level, this has been a time of developing important connections between disciplines that had been separated for decades, and deepening collaboration between colleagues around the world.

The celebration was kicked off in our last issue, which featured an interview of Oliver Turnbull by Christian Salas (Salas & Palmer-Cancel, 2019), where Oliver and Christian discussed a number of central ideas that have emerged in the neuropsychoanalysis community. In this issue, we expand on that foundation, with a series of invited personal essays from members of the community who have been involved with our interdisciplinary project in various ways, both individuals and coordinators of our vibrant regional groups.

In our Society Proceedings section, we invited our contributors to reflect on several questions: How has neuropsychoanalysis affected your members’ practice, thinking, or social/personal life? What has changed in the world of psychoanalysis, or in neuroscience, since the journal's founding in 1999? Has neuropsychoanalysis played any role in those changes? What are some key contributions made by our interdisciplinary dialogue to date? What issues are now ripe for exploration? Have we made any wrong turns or mistakes that need to be corrected?

Without any coordination between them, our contributors ended up distributing the answers amongst themselves, responding to these questions with a mixture of personal histories, theoretical discussions, and historical narratives about the development of our community. In this impressionistic yet comprehensive overview, the landscape of neuropsychoanalysis – its antecedents, some of the key ideas and most influential participants, and the ways in which integrating brain and mind affect clinical practice and research – emerge in a poignant and sometimes provocative way.

Santiago Palmer-Cancel  

Oliver Turnbull is a neuropsychologist and Professor of Psychology at Bangor University, Wales, UK. From 2002 to 2012 he was editor of the journal Neuropsychoanalysis, and in 2002 – with Mark Solms – he co-authored the book The Brain and the Inner World. He has published roughly 180 articles and chapters on themes related to emotion, emotion regulation, delusional beliefs, and the neuroscience of psychotherapy. Oliver has been an active member of the neuropsychoanalytic movement from its inception, witnessing its birth in South Africa in the 1980s, where he was Mark Solms’ first student. He has also observed the later development of neuropsychoanalysis, in larger communities in New York, London, and across the globe. This interview was held in April 2019, in the city of Santiago (Chile). As our community is preparing to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society, it seemed like a wonderful time to talk about the history of neuropsychoanalysis. Notably, Oliver has attended every one of the 20 Congresses. The interview has been lightly edited for publication.

Bulletin of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society

Maria Goergen

Maria Goergen

Maria Goergen   CONTACT Maria Sonia Goergen msonia12@gmail.com

NPSA South Brazil Group

As the oldest member of the South Brazil Group, and a founding member of the International Society of Neuropsychoanalysis, I invited the members of our group to introduce themselves to you, the reader, as you may be from the region and not know how to get in touch or to dive into the field! My name is Maria Sonia Goergen, MD, and you can read about me at another section.

As we come from various regions in the South, we will start with a few here and continue in the next bulletin.

Fabio Thá

In the heat of the debate about lay analysis, Freud wrote: “I only want to feel assured that the therapy will not destroy the science.” This is a real risk for psychoanalysis, not only for its therapeutic dimension, but mainly for its historical characteristics since it is a discipline that has grown on the fringes of official “science.” We know that this marginal position was never desired by Freud, who always fought for psychoanalysis to remain within the scientific community. Therefore, it is essential for psychoanalysts not to alienate themselves from the scientific discussions of their time, to be willing to dialogue and expose themselves to criticism. They should not view their theory as a dogmatic body of knowledge but as a scaffold in the construction of the theoretical building. This attitude is opposed to the tendency of the organized groups (and with analysts it is not different) to close themselves off and stick to unquestionable dogmas.

As far as I know, after Freud, only twice has psychoanalysis opened to the scientific debate of the day. The first time was in the 1950s, when Jacques Lacan promoted its rapprochement with the formalism that was then announced as the great tool for understanding mental processes. However, the Lacanian movement suffered the same fate of the groups, isolating itself from the scientific debate.

The second time was in the 1990s when neuroscience and psychoanalysis set out to build bridges between the two disciplines. As a leading movement in this effort comes neuropsychoanalysis, a great forum for debate, where differences are welcomed, productive criticism is cultivated, and the theoretical advance in understanding our object is already a reality. The journey just described above could be told in the first person, since it was also a path I followed. Having met neuropsychoanalysis, I am a member of the NPSA society since 2009; I’ve attended the 15th Congress in New York, 2014; the 17th Congress in Chicago, 2016, where I gave an oral presentation entitled The splitting of the ego; the 18th Congress in London, 2017, and the 19th Congress in México City, 2018. At the Mexico Congress I presented, along with Eduardo B. N. da Silveira and Tiago B. N. da Silveira, an oral presentation entitled The hysterical symptom: A proposal of articulation between the Freudian theory and the Bayesian account.
